newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Daunting task awaits new Liberian leader.
newsitem.headline: Daunting task awaits new Liberian leader.

text.p: Tubmanburg has little to show for a city in the heartland of Liberia's once thriving iron ore and diamond mining industry.

Yet in Saturday's presidential election, its people voted massively for Charles Taylor, the man who started the seven-year civil war that devastated Tubmanburg along with the rest of the West African country.
"We have no electricity, no public toilets only five elementary schools and no high school," lamented Mayor T. Varney Lewis, a 69-year-old retired army general.

An hour's drive west of the capital Monrovia, Tubmanburg witnessed some of the most ferocious fighting in the war launched in 1989 by Taylor and was largely reduced to a rubble of shell-shattered houses.
The general hospital, Liberia's second largest medical centre before the war, was looted bare by militia fighters in 1995. It now offers only outpatient services.
Town residents eagerly tell a visitor how they voted on Saturday, and their reasons largely explain Taylor's stunning electoral showing.

Latest official results showed Taylor with an unassailable lead of 75 percent of votes, against less than 10 for his closest rival, Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf. She was not tainted by the war and had been expected to do well.
"My reason for voting for him first of all is that he brought the war. He is the only man who can stand up to the other warlords," said farmer Johnson Zumo.
Zumo said he watched Tubmanburg change hands among raiding guerrilla groups more than 50 times since the ULIMO militia wrested it from Taylor's National Patriotic Party in 1992.

"I lived here throughout the war. When Taylor was in charge here everything was alright. I could farm and do whatever I wanted without intimidation. So if he's in charge of Liberia everything will be alright," he said.
City council worker Zabon Gbanja said more than half Tubmanburg's pre-war population of about 50,000 fled after Taylor lost control.
This was no time for a woman to rule Liberia, he said.

"You put a woman in charge here, it won't take even two months before she is overthrown. We don't want to be like Sierra Leone where they put a guy in charge who knows nothing about the gun," Gbanja said.
Junior officers allied with rebels seized power in neighbouring Sierra Leone last April, overthrowing president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah who was elected after a five-year civil war.
Mayor Lewis listed his city's development needs that he expects Taylor to address quickly.
"The city has not been laid out. What you see here is what the Liberian Mining Company did. So before we rebuild the city we have to have it laid out properly," he said.
Lewis was standing in front of the city hall surrounded by his officials forced to abandon their offices because of noisy work to repair the leaking roof.

"The owner of the building is in Monrovia," said council administrative officer Sando G. Sirleaf. "He came here two weeks ago and asked us to maintain the building. He doesn't ask for rent because he knows we have no money. Staff were last paid in December."
He took a look at the ramshackle building and shook his head, saying: "So this is the seat of government."
The flag over the city hall was stolen last week. But next door a brand new Lone Star fluttered in front of a neat building -- the county headquarters of Taylor's National Patriotic Party.
"We're all sitting patiently and waiting to see what Taylor will do," Sirleaf said. "We'll be looking at reconstruction and then human development. Children have to go back to school."
Taylor, 49, faces the daunting task of convincing foreign donors to come up with the cash needed to rebuild the infrastructure and revive the economy.

"It's really going to be a difficult process," U.S. ambasador William Milam told Voice of America radio in Monrovia. "I fear that among other things the expectation of the public will run ahead of the ability of any (Liberian) government or donor government to deliver."
Most foreign businesses have long fled Liberia. An explosion of warfare in the capital in April 1996 in which Taylor played a leading role triggered looting of all commercial houses.

Major donors, including the United States which poured more foreign aid into Liberia than in any other Sub-Saharan African state before the war, are conditioning fresh assistance to the new leadership's willingness to forge reconciliation.

Liberia's foreign debt, though just over $2 billion, is a big burden in per capita terms. Taylor will need to do a deal with creditors, notably the International Monetary Fund and the African Development Bank.
Milam said Washington was willing to help "a government that is credibly elected, accepted by the people of Liberia, to reconstruct the country".
There are increasing signs that others are already taking a gamble on Liberia, judging by the number of South African mining executives scouting deals in Monrovia.

A new private television network started broadcasting in Monrovia this week, joining a growing number of commercial radio stations. The telephone service is being revamped and newspapers said Taylor had pledged to reactivate Monrovia's electricity supply before his expected August 2 inauguration.
